strongest_angle: The 2026 Steger v. Willis ruling affirms that using physical force against a citizen who is not resisting arrest—even if they are being obnoxious and cursing at officers on their own porch—is a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

key_facts.fact: In Steger v. Willis, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed that Officer Steven Willis used excessive force when he slammed a gate into Melvin Steger and punched him twice after Steger cursed at him.
key_facts.source_name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

key_facts.fact: The court found that Steger did not pose an imminent threat to the officer because an iron gate separated them and Steger made no attempt to leave his front porch.
key_facts.source_name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

key_facts.fact: The triggering event for the use of force was Steger yelling 'Fuck you!' to Officer Willis after being asked not to cuss.
key_facts.source_name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

key_facts.fact: The court ruled that a suspect has a clearly established constitutional right to be free from physical force by police when they are not resisting efforts to apprehend them.
key_facts.source_name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

key_facts.fact: The U.S. Supreme Court previously held in City of Houston v. Hill that the First Amendment protects a significant amount of verbal criticism and challenge directed at police officers.
key_facts.source_name: Supreme Court of the United States

named_entities.name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
